content: Hello, everybody, I am new to the Zulip server, so forgive me if I may have created a new thread that could coincide with an existing thread. There are too much stuff here and reading them all will take me years. I thought it might be easier if somebody can point me to an existing thread if the topic already exists. Thank you very much.

I created this thread because I have repeatedly encountered a structural pattern in several very different mathematical settings, and I would like to understand whether it already has a standard categorical formulation.

My motivation comes from comparing two independently developed theories—one concerning the relational realization of physical structure and another concerning the organization of living systems. Although their concrete mathematics is quite different, both appear to require more than the commutativity of individual diagrams.

In both cases, the admissible objects, morphisms, and transformations are constrained by a larger governing structure. Individual coherent diagrams are necessary, but they are not sufficient. A candidate construction may satisfy local coherence while still being inadmissible because it fails to remain compatible with the surrounding family of structures.

This led me to the tentative idea that coherence may sometimes play the role of an admissibility constraint rather than merely a consistency condition. I am interested in whether this intuition corresponds to an established categorical notion—perhaps involving double categories, fibrations, indexed categories, coherence spaces, or something else entirely—or whether it is simply a misleading way of looking at familiar constructions.

At this stage I am not advocating new terminology or proposing a theorem. My goal is to understand whether category theory already provides the right language for this phenomenon, and, if so, where I should be looking.

Any pointers to existing concepts, examples, or literature would be greatly appreciated.
What do you mean by an 'admissibility constraint'?

Can coherence itself function as an admissibility constraint, rather than merely as a consistency condition?

The motivation is a recurring pattern where locally coherent diagrams are still not considered admissible unless they remain compatible with a larger governing family of structures. I am interested in whether this already has a standard categorical formulation or whether I am simply rediscovering an existing idea under different language.

Rather than duplicate the discussion across multiple forums, I would be grateful for comments on the original thread here:

https://categorytheory.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/229156-theory.3A-applied-category-theory/topic/Category.20Coherence.20as.20Admissibility.20Constraints/with/626329058

Pointers to relevant concepts, examples, or literature would be especially appreciated.

I am trying to understand whether monoidal double categories provide the right language for a distinction that has arisen in my work.

At the local level, I have squares whose objects and boundary morphisms satisfy the requirements needed for each individual square to be admissible.

But I do not necessarily want to impose the full coherence structure on every object or morphism independently from the outset. Instead, when several individually admissible squares are assembled, I want additional coherence conditions to constrain the objects, morphisms, and squares jointly.

So schematically I have in mind:

admissible individual squares
→ assemblies of squares
→ higher coherence selecting admissible assemblies

Is this naturally expressible using a monoidal double category, or are the coherence conditions in a monoidal double category of a different character because they are already built into the ambient structure?

I am particularly interested in whether there is a standard framework in which local square-level admissibility is distinguished from higher-order admissibility of a whole configuration.
What do you mean by "admissibility"?

Heh, I hadn't known that @Matteo Capucci (he/him) asked the exact same question!

It goes to show: if you talk in ways that sound technical but don't have any meaning to mathematicians, they will want to know exactly what you mean.
@John Dai please don't double post. People who want to reply to your thread will do so here
Understand. I posted a shorter version of my question here after I realized it might be relevant to this discussion.

Matteo Capucci (he/him) said:

What do you mean by an 'admissibility constraint'?

By “admissibility” I mean admissibility relative to extra coherence conditions imposed on a functor.

Suppose we have two categories A and B and a functor

F: A -> B.

As an ordinary functor, F sends every object and morphism of A to B. But now suppose we require F to be symmetric monoidal. Then we also require coherent structure maps like

F(X) tensor F(Y) ~= F(X tensor Y)

and

1_B ~= F(1_A),

with the usual compatibility conditions for associativity, units, and symmetry.

So the issue is not whether an object or morphism has an image under F. The issue is whether a proposed collection of structures in A can be carried to B in a way compatible with all of those extra coherence conditions.

That is what I mean by admissible: a structure is admissible if its image can participate in the full symmetric-monoidal structure of F.

So, schematically:

ordinary functorial image
vs.
image compatible with the required coherence.

Equivalently, some data may map perfectly well under the underlying functor, but fail to extend to a symmetric-monoidal realization because the tensor products, symmetries, or compositions cannot all be made compatible at once.

My point is simply that, if B is viewed as the space of realizations of A under a functor F, then requiring F merely to preserve the relevant squares admits a relatively broad class of realizations in B. Requiring F to be symmetric monoidal imposes additional compatibility conditions across those images, thereby selecting a smaller class of admissible realizations.

Please do press me for clarification. It is a delicate balance between defining everything as if nobody knows anything and presuming everybody already knows everything. I will try to be sensitive and conscientious. I promise.

But it is a fair point that “admissibility” is not a standard categorical term. But that is why the question is in an “applied” thread. By an “admissible square” I mean a commutative square whose objects and morphisms satisfy whatever local structural constraints are imposed in the problem at hand.

What I am trying to isolate is the distinction between local admissibility of individual squares and stronger compatibility conditions that arise only when a family of such squares is considered together.

So the question is: starting from a class of locally valid squares, what categorical structure lets us impose additional coherence conditions on the family as a whole, thereby selecting a smaller class of jointly realizable configurations?

I should clarify that I am not asking whether this two-stage construction is possible; I have a constructive example in which locally admissible squares are assembled and then subjected to additional higher-order coherence conditions that restrict the jointly realizable configurations.

My question is whether category theorists have already developed a systematic framework for doing this in general: starting from locally admissible cells, then imposing higher coherence as an additional selection principle on their assemblies.

John: you are right I could be more clear about what I meant by “admissibility”. I was using some terms that were natural and intuitive for the specifics problems I have been working on, but can be meaningless in a more general setting, because “admissibility” could mean different things in different settings. I think you were really pressing me for a specific example.

For an example, if we naively model a natural language as a mapping between generic syntactic rules without strong typing to semantic expressions then the semantic image may contain funny expressions like “an ant can eat a universe”. This expression has to be inadmissible. But how? One way to do this is to think about collecting all possible expressions involving ants and universes that can legitimately descend from the syntactic category and show that they can not be logically consistent as a whole. This is one admissibility problem. Its resolution may not require appealing to higher order coherence conditions.

I doubt that the nonsense-ness of the sentence "an ant can eat a universe" is something that can be expressed syntactically. It is a sentence I could imagine reading in e.g. a Terry Pratchett book. It's not on the level of nonsense of "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously." Am I misunderstanding your point?

By an “admissible square” I mean a commutative square whose objects and morphisms satisfy whatever local structural constraints are imposed in the problem at hand.

this is so general so as to not mean much to me. Please give a pair of contrasting examples coming purely from mathematics using terminology that a category theorist can be assumed to be familiar with.

locally valid squares

does valid = admissible?

Syntactically, that nonsense sentence is just Eat: NP x NP -> sentence, so it is legit. But at the semantic level, it becomes eat: Entity x Entity -> proposition with each Entity assigned a specific meaning. Now the crucial point is that a specific meaning entails logical obligations. So the sentence “an ant can eat the universe” is inadmissible not because it is illegitimate by itself, but because it can not be compatible with all other individually/locally legitimate semantic expressions involving an ant and a universe.

My bad. I think you, John and Matteo are all correct in questioning whether I have defined the “inadmissible square” clearly enough. The existence of a square itself should imply commutativity so the notion of an admissible square is redundant. what I should have said is this: consider a collection of squares each representing a point-wise object/morphism square, then such a collection may not be admissible once the objects on one side of the functorial mapping are assigned specific semantic meaning (human language, physics, etc).

Basically the way I put it earlier I was conflating the notion of categorical admissibility / validity with the notion of semantic admissibility / validity. My clarification relating to the non-sense sentence “an ant can eat the universe” is a good illustrative example. If “ant” and “universe” remain abstract labels without any semantic meaning with logical consequences, then we can form a legitimate square mapping a syntactic expression to this semantic expression. Now, even after ant and universe have been assigned specific meanings, there is a question of whether we should assert that the syntactic to semantic square is still admissible / valid on its own but not compatible with other admissible / valid squares or whether we should assert that given the assigned semantic meanings this square is simply not admissible / valid any more. Joe Moeller appears to be leaning toward the latter, and I was too. But I now believe that I am leaning toward the former: the squares are locally admissible / valid. What makes the sentence a non-sentence is because it is not compatible with some other squares under a consistent assignment of semantic meaning to all objects and morphisms.
These are not mathematical examples, so I don't know what you mean. Perhaps you are not intending there to be examples from mathematics, in which case I have no feedback to give

the notion of categorical admissibility / validity

David, I need some help here. I am not a mathematician. I am a theoretical physicist with descent grounding in complex analysis, differential geometry, group symmetry and topology, and I have a keen interest in category theory as a way to constrain physical models. The idea is that you have a syntactic category and a functorial mapping to a semantic category. The question is: what makes the semantic category a logically consistent language that describes reality?

Let me try to define the language problem mathematically:

For language, the mathematical problem is not merely to define an interpretation functor. It is to determine which syntactically valid expressions remain semantically admissible once interpreted meanings impose type and consistency constraints.

A concise formulation is:

Given a syntactic category C_syn, a semantic category C_sem, an interpretation functor

F: C_syn -> C_sem,

and a category of consistent semantic typings

p: E_cons -> C_sem,

determine the subcategories D of C_syn for which the restricted interpretation

F|D: D -> C_sem

admits a lift

F_hat_D: D -> E_cons

with

p o F_hat_D = F|D.

Then study the admissibility poset

A = { D subseteq C_syn : F|D admits such a lift }.

The core questions are:

  • when does a global lift exist on all of C_syn?
  • if not, do maximal admissible subcategories exist?
  • is there a unique largest admissible subcategory?
  • how can it be constructed from local semantic typing constraints?
  • what conditions guarantee closure of admissibility under composition?

In plain language:

The problem is to determine the largest fragment of syntactically valid language whose semantic interpretation can be assigned mutually compatible meanings everywhere at once.
I have isolated this problem also because it may have some interesting implications for LLM training and/or interpretations

I was hoping that mathematicians would say: hey John, you are not stating the problem in a form that we can understand. But based on what you are saying, perhaps this is the mathematical problem you are trying to solve? As a DYI plumber, I know that once I have defined the problem, I have already solved 85-90% of that problem. So repeatedly asking me, a non-mathematician, to state a problem in a mathematically prestine fashion feels like shutting me down for being a non-mathematician — as if I don’t belong here. That is not the best attitude toward a fellow truth seeker. :blush:

@John Dai As you could probably imagine, we've had a few instances in this community of new people showing up and then simply copy pasting nonsense from some LLM. To earlier instances of this, we largely responded with genuine attempts to meaningfully engage with the person. We actually ended up spending a lot of time chasing things down that turned out to be pure mist. After this happening more times, we've sorta landed on a strategy of identifying the core concepts that the poster seems to be working around, and then asking for a rigorous definition. This seems to be a good strategy for weeding out people that have no idea what's going on. To be super clear, the community doesn't have a single unified opinion on the use of LLMs, but we do agree that nobody is interested in sifting through tomes of slop hoping to find a kernel of mild interest. To be ultra-mega clear, I'm not accusing you of this at all. I'm not evaluating your post in any way. I just felt like sharing where our attitude might be coming from. We do ultimately want to be welcoming to people of all backgrounds interested in category theory. We can always do better on being more welcoming, and we should also remain vigilant on keeping garbage out.

Hi @John Dai,

I believe I understand what you are after, so I will try to help formalize your idea.

In particular, I think the following intuition you expressed can be made mathematically precise:

This led me to the tentative idea that coherence may sometimes play the role of an admissibility constraint rather than merely a consistency condition.

and similarly:

Can coherence itself function as an admissibility constraint, rather than merely as a consistency condition?

First, every monoid can be viewed as a category with a single object. Using this, I will denote the multiplicative monoid Z/2Z={0,1}\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}=\{0,1\}Z/2Z={0,1} by Csem\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{sem}}Csem​, referring to the semantic category that you mentioned.

Then I will denote by W\mathcal{W}W the list of words in my language, say a tokenization of English, and by ΣW\Sigma\mathcal{W}ΣW the free monoid generated by W\mathcal{W}W.

For example,

W={"An"," ant"," can"," eat"," a"," universe",…}.\mathcal{W}=\{\texttt{"An"},\texttt{" ant"},\texttt{" can"},\texttt{" eat"},\texttt{" a"},\texttt{" universe"},\ldots\}.W={"An"," ant"," can"," eat"," a"," universe",…}.

Because each of these words makes sense individually, we can assign a valid semantic value to each of these atomic syntactic components:

F("An")=1,F(" ant")=1,…F(\texttt{"An"})=1,\quad F(\texttt{" ant"})=1,\quad\dotsF("An")=1,F(" ant")=1,…

However, making the mapping FFF preserve the underlying monoid structures becomes more difficult as we move from these local pieces toward more global expressions.

We may certainly have

F("An ant")=1,F(" can eat")=1,F(" a universe")=1,…F(\texttt{"An ant"})=1,\quad F(\texttt{" can eat"})=1,\quad F(\texttt{" a universe"})=1,\quad\dotsF("An ant")=1,F(" can eat")=1,F(" a universe")=1,…

and we can even consider intersecting segments such as

F("An ant can eat")=1,F(" can eat a universe")=1,…F(\texttt{"An ant can eat"})=1,\quad F(\texttt{" can eat a universe"})=1,\quad\dotsF("An ant can eat")=1,F(" can eat a universe")=1,…

But the multiplication 1⋅1=11\cdot 1=11⋅1=1 in Csem\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{sem}}Csem​ is not compatible with the complete local-to-global transition when we build the larger sentence, since we would want

F("An ant can eat a universe")=0.F(\texttt{"An ant can eat a universe"})=0.F("An ant can eat a universe")=0.

I think this is very close to what you mean when you say that locally admissible structures may fail to remain admissible once they are considered as part of a larger family.

This is where categories become useful, because they allow us to restrict the monoid multiplication to sparser compositions.

It is possible to define a category C\mathcal{C}C whose set of objects is ΣW\Sigma\mathcal{W}ΣW and whose arrows are triples in ΣW×3\Sigma\mathcal{W}^{\times 3}ΣW×3, where

(m,a,b):a→b(m,a,b):a\to b(m,a,b):a→b

is an arrow in C\mathcal{C}C.

Composition is defined by

(n,b,c)∘(m,a,b)=(m⋅n,a,c).(n,b,c)\circ(m,a,b)=(m\cdot n,a,c).(n,b,c)∘(m,a,b)=(m⋅n,a,c).

Examples of arrows in C\mathcal{C}C are

("An ant","An"," can"):"An"→" can"(\texttt{"An ant"},\texttt{"An"},\texttt{" can"}):\texttt{"An"}\to\texttt{" can"}("An ant","An"," can"):"An"→" can"

and

(" can eat"," can"," a"):" can"→" a".(\texttt{" can eat"},\texttt{" can"},\texttt{" a"}):\texttt{" can"}\to\texttt{" a"}.(" can eat"," can"," a"):" can"→" a".

Their composition is therefore

("An ant can eat","An"," a"):"An"→" a".(\texttt{"An ant can eat"},\texttt{"An"},\texttt{" a"}):\texttt{"An"}\to\texttt{" a"}.("An ant can eat","An"," a"):"An"→" a".

Note: This category is inherently related to autoregressive language models because the category-theoretic target of an arrow (m,a,b):a→b(m,a,b): a \to b(m,a,b):a→b corresponds to what we call a "target" during the training of an LLM for a given prompt mmm and context aaa.

The categorical structure of C\mathcal{C}C now gives us more local control over semantics because we can control which contexts and targets are allowed.

For instance, we may impose

F(" ant can"⟶" ant can eat a"" universe")=0.F(\texttt{" ant can"}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\texttt{" ant can eat a"}}\texttt{" universe"})=0.F(" ant can"⟶" ant can eat a"​" universe")=0.

This means that if we compose any arrow targeting " ant can"\texttt{" ant can"}" ant can" with the arrow above, then the resulting sentence will be semantically invalid.

This seems to connect quite directly with another formulation you gave:

What I am trying to isolate is the distinction between local admissibility of individual squares and stronger compatibility conditions that arise only when a family of such squares is considered together.

In this toy construction, the corresponding distinction is between assigning semantic values to individual pieces and requiring those values to remain compatible under the compositions that assemble them into larger structures.

The main problem then becomes:

  • Does FFF even exist and, if so, is it a functor?

  • If not, does there exist a subcategory D⊆CD\subseteq\mathcal{C}D⊆C such that the restriction of FFF to DDD is a functor D→CsemD \to \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{sem}} D→Csem​?

This also seems very close to your later question about finding the largest fragment of a syntactically valid language whose semantic interpretations can remain mutually compatible everywhere at once.

There are a few points where I am less certain, and I would be interested to know whether they match what you have in mind.

First, I am wondering whether some of the squares you mentioned could arise from the different ways of composing smaller linguistic pieces into the same larger expression.

For example, in the category C\mathcal{C}C above, consider the arrows

f=("An ant","An"," can"):"An"→" can"f=(\texttt{"An ant"},\texttt{"An"},\texttt{" can"}):\texttt{"An"}\to\texttt{" can"}f=("An ant","An"," can"):"An"→" can"

g=(" can eat a"," can"," universe"):" can"→" universe"g=(\texttt{" can eat a"},\texttt{" can"},\texttt{" universe"}):\texttt{" can"}\to\texttt{" universe"}g=(" can eat a"," can"," universe"):" can"→" universe"

and

h=("An ant can","An"," eat"):"An"→" eat"h=(\texttt{"An ant can"},\texttt{"An"},\texttt{" eat"}):\texttt{"An"}\to\texttt{" eat"}h=("An ant can","An"," eat"):"An"→" eat"

k=(" eat a"," eat"," universe"):" eat"→" universe".k=(\texttt{" eat a"},\texttt{" eat"},\texttt{" universe"}):\texttt{" eat"}\to\texttt{" universe"}.k=(" eat a"," eat"," universe"):" eat"→" universe".

Then we have two different compositional paths:

"An"⟶"An ant"" can"⟶" can eat a"" universe"\texttt{"An"}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\texttt{"An ant"}}\texttt{" can"}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\texttt{" can eat a"}}\texttt{" universe"}"An"⟶"An ant"​" can"⟶" can eat a"​" universe"

and

"An"⟶"An ant can"" eat"⟶" eat a"" universe".\texttt{"An"}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\texttt{"An ant can"}}\texttt{" eat"}\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\texttt{" eat a"}}\texttt{" universe"}."An"⟶"An ant can"​" eat"⟶" eat a"​" universe".

Both compositions give

g∘f=k∘h=("An ant can eat a","An"," universe").g\circ f=k\circ h=(\texttt{"An ant can eat a"},\texttt{"An"},\texttt{" universe"}).g∘f=k∘h=("An ant can eat a","An"," universe").

So f,g,h,kf,g,h,kf,g,h,k form a commutative square. In this example, the square expresses the fact that two different local decompositions assemble into the same larger syntactic construction.

I am wondering whether this is close to what you mean when you write:

At the local level, I have squares whose objects and boundary morphisms satisfy the requirements needed for each individual square to be admissible.

But I do not necessarily want to impose the full coherence structure on every object or morphism independently from the outset. Instead, when several individually admissible squares are assembled, I want additional coherence conditions to constrain the objects, morphisms, and squares jointly.

admissible individual squares
→ assemblies of squares
→ higher coherence selecting admissible assemblies

If so, then I would interpret one square such as the one above as expressing a local compatibility between two ways of composing the same expression.

The next step would be to consider many such squares at once. Different squares could overlap by sharing objects or arrows, and the same longer expression could appear through several different chains of compositions. The question would then no longer be only whether each individual square commutes, but whether all of these local commutative squares can be assembled into one jointly compatible structure.

That seems very close to your distinction between an individually admissible square and an admissible assembly of squares.

I am less certain about whether a monoidal double category is the right structure for expressing that second step, but I think this example may at least isolate the distinction you are trying to capture.
